However, the proposed finding is about missing test coverage rather than a concrete bug/security/correctness defect introduced by the code itself; the diff does not show a project requirement that tests must be added for such changes. Therefore it’s not a verifiable functional problem in the code, just a process/quality suggestion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:31-38 — no check on booking.status, allowing guests to be added to cancelled, rejected, or pending bookings, which sends CONFIRMED ics attachments for nonexistent events

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the booking is fetched by id only (no where-clause or runtime guard on booking.status), and the handler proceeds to (1) create new attendee records, (2) call eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees, and (3) send emails that generate ICS payloads with status: "CONFIRMED" (see new attendee/organizer add-guests email templates). Therefore, the diff does allow adding guests (and sending confirmed ICS updates) even if the booking is cancelled/rejected/pending, because no status check exists in the shown code path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:66-74 — blacklist check and attendee dedupe are case-sensitive while blacklist is lowercased, allowing bypass via case variation (e.g. Spam@x.com bypasses spam@x.com block) and duplicate attendees

addGuests.handler.ts:160-165 — seat-based event types only copy seat metadata for emails; no capacity check or seat-booking association, allowing overbooking beyond seatsPerTimeSlot and potential email leakage when seatsShowAttendees is false
addGuests.schema.ts:5 — guests array has no .max() limit, enabling unbounded attendees and an email-bomb/DoS vector against mail and calendar providers

adjudication.rationale: The new TRPC input schema `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` accepts `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no upper bound. The `addGuestsHandler` then uses that array to (a) `createMany` attendees in the DB and (b) calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, which loops over `calendarEvent.attendees` and sends emails. There is no server-side cap on number of guests, so an authorized caller (organizer/attendee/team admin/owner) can submit an extremely large array, causing large DB writes plus a burst of outbound emails/ICS updates (DoS / email-bomb potential).

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:167-170 — email send failure is swallowed with only a console.log and reported as success, so guests may never be notified while the user sees a success toast

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts, the code wraps `await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests);` in a try/catch that only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` on failure and does not rethrow (lines ~167-170 in the new file). The handler then proceeds to return `{ message: "Guests added" }`, causing the TRPC mutation to resolve successfully. On the client, `onSuccess` shows a success toast (`showToast(t("guests_added"), "success")`) and closes the dialog. This means email notification failures are silently ignored and users are told the operation succeeded, even if guests were not notified.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Authorization check uses && instead of || in isTeamAdminOrOwner, requiring BOTH admin AND owner roles so team admins are silently locked out of guest management on team bookings

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which requires the user to be both a team admin and a team owner. The variable name and the subsequent permission gate (`if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee)`) indicate the intended logic is “admin OR owner”. As written, a team admin who is not also an owner will fail `isTeamAdminOrOwner` and be denied unless they are also the organizer or an attendee, effectively locking out admins from this action on team bookings.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No server-side uniqueness enforcement for duplicates within the input array; duplicate emails in the guests input create duplicate attendee rows and cause duplicate emails and ICS REQUESTs to be sent
Case-sensitive email comparison: blacklist entries are lowercased but incoming guest emails are not, allowing blacklist bypass via casing and defeating the duplicate attendee check
No booking.status invariant check, allowing guests to be added to cancelled or rejected bookings, after which ICS REQUEST/CONFIRMED updates resurrect the cancelled event in attendees' calendars

adjudication.rationale: The new `addGuestsHandler` mutates any booking found by `id` without checking any booking lifecycle/state (e.g., cancelled/rejected). It always updates attendees (`prisma.booking.update(... attendees.createMany ...)`), calls `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`, and then sends add-guest emails whose ICS payload hardcodes `status: "CONFIRMED"` and `method: "REQUEST"` in both `attendee-add-guests-email.ts` and `organizer-add-guests-email.ts`. So if the booking is cancelled/rejected, this endpoint can still add guests and emit CONFIRMED calendar updates, which is a concrete correctness issue introduced/left unguarded by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Seated event types are handled but seat capacity is never checked against seatsPerTimeSlot and no BookingSeat records are created for new attendees, allowing overbooking and inconsistent seat data

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an `addGuests` mutation that appends new `attendees` to an existing booking via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and then updates calendars/emails. While the handler copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` onto the `CalendarEvent`, the diff does not show (or reference) any seat-capacity enforcement mechanism or any `BookingSeat` model/table usage. The claim that seat capacity must be checked here and that `BookingSeat` records must be created is therefore not directly verifiable from the diff alone and depends on assumptions about how “seated event types” are implemented elsewhere.

adjudication_records.issue_text: isAttendee grants write access for any attendee to add arbitrary guests and send emails as the organizer, an email amplification vector beyond the stated organizer-guest-management scope

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the authorization check explicitly allows any booking attendee to perform the mutation: `const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);` and then `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN;`. That means any attendee (not just the organizer/admin) can add arbitrary guest emails to the booking (`prisma.booking.update(... attendees.createMany ...)`) and it will also trigger calendar updates (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`) and broadcast emails (`sendAddGuestsEmails`) which are composed as organizer/meeting emails. This is a real permission expansion and can be used as an email amplification/spam vector by any attendee of a booking.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EventManager is built with the requesting user's credentials rather than the booking owner's, so for non-organizer callers the calendar update targets the wrong account, and it throws after the DB write without try/catch leaving the mutation half-applied

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts` the mutation allows non-organizer callers (`isAttendee` or team admin/owner) to execute. However, it builds `EventManager` with the requesting `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`, not the booking owner/organizer (`booking.user` / `booking.userId`). That means a non-organizer will attempt calendar attendee updates using their own connected calendar credentials, which is the wrong account for updating the organizer’s event and can fail or affect the wrong calendar. Also, the DB update (`prisma.booking.update` with `createMany`) happens before `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and that call is not wrapped in try/catch/transaction; if it throws, the mutation errors after persisting new attendees, leaving state half-applied (DB updated, external calendar not).

adjudication_records.issue_text: AddGuestsDialog's isInvalidEmail state is never reset on the success path, causing a stale error banner to display the next time the dialog opens

adjudication.rationale: In AddGuestsDialog, `isInvalidEmail` is set to `true` when validation fails (`setIsInvalidEmail(true)`), and it is only reset in the Cancel button handler. In the mutation `onSuccess`, the code closes the dialog and resets `multiEmailValue`, but does not call `setIsInvalidEmail(false)`. Since the dialog component remains mounted (it’s always rendered in `BookingListItem` and visibility is controlled via `open={isOpenDialog}`), `isInvalidEmail` can persist as `true` across closes/opens, causing the error banner to show immediately the next time the dialog opens.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The isTeamAdminOrOwner check requires the caller to be BOTH admin AND owner instead of either, denying legitimate team admins with FORBIDDEN

adjudication.rationale:
In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&`:

```ts
const isTeamAdminOrOwner =
  (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0)) &&
  (await isTeamOwner(user.id, booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0));
```

This requires the user to be both a team admin and the team owner. Given the variable name and the authorization guard (`if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) ... FORBIDDEN`), this will deny access to legitimate team admins who are not owners (and vice versa, if owner isn’t considered admin by `isTeamAdmin`). The finding accurately identifies a real logic/permission bug introduced in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Admin/owner check consults booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0 instead of booking.teamId, so team bookings with deleted event types become unmanageable except by the original organizer

adjudication.rationale: In the new `addGuestsHandler`, the permission check derives the team context from `booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0`. The proposed finding assumes there is a `booking.teamId` field that should be used instead, and further assumes a “deleted event type” scenario where `booking.eventType` becomes null. Neither of those is verifiable from the diff: no `booking.teamId` property is referenced or shown, and whether `eventType` can be deleted/nullable in a way that leaves a team booking is not established here. Therefore the finding is speculative rather than a concrete, diff-proven defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Server does not enforce guest uniqueness within the guests array; the invariant lives only in a client-side zod schema, allowing direct API callers to create duplicate attendee rows

adjudication.rationale: Yes. On the server, `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` only validates `guests` as `z.array(z.string().email())` (no uniqueness refinement). In `addGuestsHandler`, `uniqueGuests` is computed with `guests.filter(...)` only excluding emails that already exist in `booking.attendees` or are blacklisted; it does not dedupe duplicates within the incoming `guests` array itself. Therefore a direct API caller can submit `guests: ["a@b.com", "a@b.com"]` (when not already an attendee) and both entries remain in `uniqueGuests`, leading `createMany` to attempt inserting duplicate attendee rows. The client-side dialog adds a uniqueness refine, but that protection is not enforced server-side.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blacklist check is case-sensitive: blacklist entries are lowercased but the guest email is not, making the blacklist bypassable by case variation
Unbounded guests array with no max(), rate limit, or attendee cap lets any attendee mail-bomb the organizer, team, and prior guests in repeated calls

adjudication.rationale: The new `addGuests` mutation accepts `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.max()` (server-side) and the handler allows any existing attendee (`isAttendee`) to call it. The handler then (a) creates attendees via `createMany` for all `uniqueGuests` (also unbounded) and (b) sends emails to the organizer, each team member, and **every attendee** via `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` (note it even passes the original unbounded `guests` array). There is no attendee-cap check, batching, or rate limiting in the diff, so a malicious attendee can submit very large arrays and/or repeat calls to generate a large number of outbound emails (mail-bomb) to organizer/team/prior attendees.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Check-then-insert against stale data with no transaction or UNIQUE(bookingId, email) constraint causes duplicate attendees under concurrent requests

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuestsHandler`, the code reads the current attendees (`booking.attendees`) and filters `uniqueGuests` based on that snapshot, then performs `prisma.booking.update(... attendees.createMany ...)` without a transaction/locking and without `skipDuplicates`. This is a classic non-atomic check-then-insert: concurrent requests can both observe that an email is not yet an attendee and both insert it, producing duplicate attendee rows unless the DB enforces a UNIQUE constraint on (bookingId, email) (not shown in the diff). Additionally, the server-side `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` does not enforce uniqueness, so a single request can include duplicate emails and `createMany` would attempt to insert duplicates as well unless constrained.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Non-atomic write-then-side-effect sequence: if the calendar update throws after attendees are persisted, a retry is rejected with BAD_REQUEST, permanently wedging the user; swallowed email errors also report success when nothing was sent

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the code persists new attendees via `prisma.booking.update(... createMany ...)` before running the side effects `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws, the mutation fails but the attendees are already stored; a retry with the same `guests` will compute `uniqueGuests` as empty (because they now exist in `booking.attendees`) and will throw `TRPCError({ code: "BAD_REQUEST", message: "emails_must_be_unique_valid" })`, preventing a straightforward retry to complete the calendar sync. Separately, `sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in a `try/catch` that only logs and does not rethrow, so the handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` even when email sending fails, meaning it can report success while no emails were sent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EventManager is constructed from the caller's credentials instead of the booking organizer's, so calendar attendee sync fails for attendee or team admin callers

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the mutation allows non-organizers to add guests (`isAttendee` or `isTeamAdminOrOwner`). However, the calendar sync uses `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user);` and constructs `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })`, where `user` is `ctx.user` (the caller), not the booking organizer (`booking.userId` / `organizer`). If an attendee (or team admin who isn’t the organizer) calls this, they likely won’t have the organizer’s calendar credentials needed to update the booking’s linked calendar event, so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` can fail or update the wrong calendar context. This mismatch is directly present in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No booking status guard: guests can be added to cancelled/rejected/pending bookings, re-sending CONFIRMED ICS invites that resurrect cancelled events on attendees' calendars

adjudication.rationale: The new `addGuestsHandler` fetches the booking (including attendees/eventType/etc.) but never checks any booking status/state (e.g., cancelled/rejected/pending) before updating attendees and triggering calendar/email side effects. It always calls `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and sends emails whose ICS payloads are hard-coded with `status: "CONFIRMED"` and `method: "REQUEST"` (see `attendee-add-guests-email.ts` and `organizer-add-guests-email.ts`). Additionally, the new UI action (`additional_guests`) is added without any visible guard based on booking status. Therefore, adding guests to non-confirmed/cancelled bookings is not prevented and could send CONFIRMED invites for bookings that shouldn’t be active.

adjudication_records.issue_text: newGuests.includes(attendee.email) decides email template by case-sensitive string match rather than an explicit 'is new' flag, breaking silently if any email normalization is introduced upstream

adjudication.rationale: In sendAddGuestsEmails, the template choice is based on `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, which is a strict, case-sensitive string equality check. Emails are effectively case-insensitive, and attendee emails may come from persisted data (DB/calendarEvent formatting) with different casing than the input `newGuests` array. That can misclassify an attendee as “not new” (or “new”) and send the wrong email template without any error. This is a concrete correctness risk inherent to the code as written, not just style.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Authorization logic in addGuests.handler.ts:57-58 uses && instead of || between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner, silently narrowing permission to admin AND owner and locking team admins (non-owners) out of the addGuests feature

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. That expression is only true when the user is BOTH a team admin and the team owner. The variable name and typical permission intent (“admin OR owner”) indicate it should be `||`; with `&&`, legitimate team admins who are not owners will fail the later permission check and be forbidden from adding guests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: isAttendee escape hatch in addGuests.handler.ts:53-62 allows any attendee to inject unlimited guests with no .max() on the array, enabling free calendar REQUEST emails to arbitrary addresses with no UI or design justification in the diff

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In the new `addGuests` mutation, any authenticated user who is an existing booking attendee (`isAttendee` computed from `booking.attendees`) is permitted to add guests (`if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN`). The input schema `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` defines `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.max(...)` or other size limit, and the handler proceeds to create attendees and then calls `sendAddGuestsEmails(...)`, which results in sending emails/ICS updates. This makes it possible for an attendee to submit an arbitrarily large list of email addresses and trigger outbound email traffic, which is a verifiable abuse/spam vector introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In addGuests.handler.ts:144-150, when caller is an attendee, EventManager is built from ctx.user credentials but evt.destinationCalendar belongs to the organizer, causing silent calendar sync failure while DB/email succeed; errors in updateCalendarAttendees are not caught

adjudication.rationale: The handler explicitly allows an attendee to call `addGuestsHandler` (`isAttendee` check), but then constructs `EventManager` from `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (the caller’s credentials) while `evt.destinationCalendar` is taken from `booking.destinationCalendar` / `booking.user.destinationCalendar` (the organizer/booking owner’s calendars). This mismatch is directly visible in the diff and can cause calendar updates to fail when the caller isn’t the organizer. Also, `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);` is not wrapped in a try/catch (only `sendAddGuestsEmails` is), so any thrown error will bubble up after the DB update has already happened, leading to inconsistent state (DB updated but calendar update failed).

adjudication_records.issue_text: No booking.status check in addGuests.handler.ts or email templates; cancelled/rejected bookings can mint CONFIRMED ics invites with status hardcoded to CONFIRMED and method REQUEST, re-confirming dead events

adjudication.rationale: The new addGuests flow never checks the booking’s lifecycle/status before updating attendees and sending emails. In addGuests.handler.ts it fetches the booking and proceeds regardless of whether it’s cancelled/rejected. The new email templates (packages/emails/templates/*-add-guests-email.ts) generate ICS payloads with `status: "CONFIRMED"` and `method: "REQUEST"` hardcoded, so invoking addGuests on a cancelled/rejected booking would still emit “confirmed” meeting requests, which can effectively re-invite/re-confirm a dead event.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blacklist comparison in addGuests.handler.ts:73-77 is case-asymmetric: blacklist emails are lowercased but the candidate guest is used raw, so differently-cased blacklisted addresses bypass the filter; same block also case-mismatches attendee dedupe causing duplicate attendee rows

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `blacklistedGuestEmails` is normalized to lowercase (`map((email) => email.toLowerCase())`), but the filter checks `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` without lowercasing `guest`. Since string comparison is case-sensitive, a blacklisted address like `test@example.com` can be bypassed by submitting `Test@Example.com`. The same applies to attendee de-dupe: it uses `guest === attendee.email` (case-sensitive), so a differently-cased email can slip through and be created as a duplicate attendee row.

adjudication_records.issue_text: sendAddGuestsEmails in email-manager.ts:545 receives raw input guests instead of the persisted uniqueGuests, so pre-existing or blacklisted attendee emails matching attendee addresses receive full AttendeeScheduledEmail confirmations instead of the 'new guests added' notice
matched_golden_ids: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same logic flaw: when deciding which attendees are “new” and should receive the add-guests email vs the scheduled email, the function uses a mismatched/incorrect guest list (raw input guests/newGuests) compared against the full persisted attendees list, leading to existing/non-new attendees being misclassified and sent the wrong email type.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AddGuestsDialog.tsx:23-27 forks the validation schema client-side instead of importing the shared server ZAddGuestsInputSchema; client enforces uniqueness via refine while server does not, so client and server accept different inputs

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows AddGuestsDialog.tsx defining a local `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` with a `.refine()` enforcing uniqueness (lines ~23-27), while the server-side `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts` defines `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` as only `z.object({ bookingId: z.number(), guests: z.array(z.string().email()) })` with no uniqueness constraint. This is a verifiable client/server validation mismatch introduced by the diff. Moreover, the handler’s `uniqueGuests` computation filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not dedupe duplicates within the `guests` input array, so the server can accept inputs the client rejects (or behave unexpectedly if duplicates are submitted).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Booking lookup in addGuests.handler.ts has no user/org scope and the post-fetch check grants write access to mere attendees, letting any attendee of any booking inject arbitrary new attendees via addGuests

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the booking is fetched solely by `id` with no user/team/org constraint (`prisma.booking.findFirst({ where: { id: bookingId } ... })`). Authorization is then decided after the fetch and explicitly allows any attendee: `const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);` and the deny condition is `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN;`. That means any authenticated user who is listed as an attendee on a booking can call this mutation and `prisma.booking.update(... attendees.createMany ...)` to add arbitrary new attendee emails. This matches the finding that “mere attendees” are granted write access to inject new attendees.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Emails sent with replyTo set to the organizer's email can target attacker-chosen addresses, creating an email-sending/spam/phishing vector with no rate limit
updateCalendarAttendees allows a non-owner attendee to mutate the organizer's calendar event attendee list

adjudication.rationale: The diff does allow an authenticated user who is an existing booking attendee to call `addGuests` (see `isAttendee` check) and it updates the booking’s attendees in the DB. However, the specific claim that this lets a non-owner attendee mutate the organizer’s calendar event attendee list via `updateCalendarAttendees` is not verifiable from the diff: `EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` implementation is not shown, and the `EventManager` here is constructed with the *current user’s* credentials (`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`), not the organizer’s, so it’s unclear it can modify the organizer’s external calendar event. Thus the proposed finding overreaches what the diff alone demonstrates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: NOT_FOUND-vs-FORBIDDEN response split allows probing which booking IDs exist

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `addGuestsHandler`, the code first queries `prisma.booking.findFirst({ where: { id: bookingId } ... })` and throws `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: "booking_not_found" })` when no booking exists. If a booking exists but the caller lacks permissions, it throws `new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN", message: "you_do_not_have_permission" })`. This distinct NOT_FOUND vs FORBIDDEN behavior lets any authenticated caller probe which `bookingId` values exist by observing the error code/message, matching the proposed finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS check is bypassed by case variation: blacklist entries are lowercased but the guest string compared is never lowercased, so blacklisted emails with uppercase characters are accepted
matched_golden_ids: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same bypass: the blacklist is normalized to lowercase but the guest email being checked is not, allowing uppercase variations to evade BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email uniqueness is enforced only client-side: the server schema has no uniqueness refinement and uniqueGuests only dedupes against existing attendees, so duplicate emails in a single request create duplicate attendee rows, corrupt the ICS/attendee list, and send duplicate emails
matched_golden_ids: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that uniqueGuests only filters against existing/blacklisted emails and does not deduplicate duplicates within the same request, allowing createMany to insert multiple attendee rows for repeated emails. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: updateCalendarAttendees runs with the requesting user's credentials instead of the booking owner's, causing silent failures (inconsistent DB/email vs calendar state) or an attacker-controlled write path in the attendee case

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the handler allows not only the organizer but also any existing attendee (`isAttendee`) to add guests. It then calls `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and constructs `EventManager` with the requesting user’s credentials (`new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })`), and uses that to run `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. The booking owner’s credentials are available in the earlier `booking` query (`include: { user: { include: { credentials: true }}}`) but are not used. This makes the calendar update depend on the requester’s integrations rather than the booking owner’s, which can cause failures when an attendee triggers the mutation (attendee likely lacks access to the organizer’s calendar event), leading to inconsistent state vs the DB update that already occurred. It also creates an attacker-controlled external-calendar write attempt path in the attendee-authorized case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && where || is required, so team admins (non-owners) fail the check and only owners satisfy it, deviating from the intended authorization matrix

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. This requires the user to be both a team admin and a team owner to pass that branch, which contradicts the variable name and the apparent intent to allow either role. As written, a team admin who is not an owner will fail authorization (and potentially an owner who isn't considered an admin would also fail), making the permission check stricter than intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: booking.eventType can be null (left-joined), causing the admin/owner check to silently evaluate against teamId 0

adjudication.rationale: In the new `addGuestsHandler`, `booking` is fetched with `include: { eventType: true }`, but the relation can be `null`/`undefined` (optional relation or deleted event type). The permission logic then computes `booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0` and passes `0` into `isTeamAdmin`/`isTeamOwner`, meaning the team admin/owner path will be evaluated against teamId `0` instead of being skipped or handled explicitly when there is no team. This is a concrete correctness issue introduced by the diff (silent wrong teamId in auth check).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Attendee rows are written to the DB before the calendar update, with no transaction and no rollback: if the calendar provider errors, guest rows persist in the DB while the calendar event and emails are never updated, leaving half-migrated state that cannot be rolled back through the application

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the code persists the new guests to the database first via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and only afterwards calls `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);`. There is no Prisma transaction wrapping these steps and no rollback logic if `updateCalendarAttendees` throws (it is not inside a try/catch). Therefore, a calendar provider/update failure would leave the DB with added attendee rows while the external calendar update (and subsequent email sending) does not complete, creating an inconsistent/partial state.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dedup check uses exact-case string equality (guest === attendee.email) with no lowercasing, so a differently-cased duplicate email permanently creates a duplicate attendee row that is emailed and added to the calendar twice, with no removal path

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, deduplication is done with strict string equality: `!booking.attendees.some((attendee) => guest === attendee.email)`. Neither `guest` nor `attendee.email` is normalized (e.g., `toLowerCase()`), and the input schema `z.string().email()` validates format but does not canonicalize case. As a result, adding `Test@Example.com` when `test@example.com` already exists will bypass the dedup filter and proceed to `attendees.createMany`, causing duplicate attendee entries and downstream effects (calendar update / emails) for what is effectively the same email in a case-insensitive system. This case-sensitivity issue is directly verifiable in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email-send failure is swallowed with only a console.log, so the handler returns 'Guests added' and the DB write succeeds while no guests or organizer are notified and no ICS REQUEST update is delivered, with no way to re-trigger the emails

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the DB update and calendar attendee update happen, then `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is wrapped in a `try/catch` that only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` and does not rethrow or return an error. The handler then returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` regardless of email delivery. This means email-send failures are silently swallowed and callers will see success even when notifications/ICS emails were not sent.
